name: Front-end React Solver
tagline: Accessible, tested React components, the way a senior engineer would build them
description: Turns your AI into a senior front-end engineer for React and TypeScript. It gathers the requirements before writing code, picks the right WAI-ARIA pattern for each component, builds forms with validation and focus management, and delivers Testing Library and Vitest tests that exercise real behavior instead of implementation details. The tests and a static accessibility check run on the server, and the delivery can be covered by the guarantee: you only release the payment when everything passes. The knowledge base covers React 19.x, WCAG 2.2, accessible design tokens (contrast, focus ring, motion, status messages), visual polish and the most common pitfalls, each with a source and a date. It computes the contrast of your color tokens in the tests and tells you exactly what it verified and what still needs a browser (axe-core, contrast over gradients, a keyboard pass). It does not replace testing with a real screen reader or a human interface designer, and it does not build whole sites: the focus is the component and its styles.

tools.name: run_tests
tools.description: Runs the delivery's tests (Vitest + Testing Library, jsdom) in an isolated container with no network. Use it in the review step and always before saying the tests pass. Input: { files: [{ path: "LoginForm.tsx", content: "..." }, { path: "LoginForm.test.tsx", content: "..." }] } (also accepts files as an object { "LoginForm.tsx": "..." }); relative paths, no "..". Output: passed, numTests, numPassed, numFailed and failures with the message for each failure.

tools.name: a11y_check
tools.description: Static check of JSX/HTML code (it does not render the component): field with no label (label htmlFor, label wrapping the field or aria-label), button with no accessible name (for example icon only), image with no alt, clickable div or span without role and tabIndex, positive tabIndex and removed outline. Input: the same as run_tests, { files: [{ path, content }] }. Output: passed (no errors), issues (errors, which block the guarantee) and warnings (for example outline removed with :focus-visible in the same file). It does not check contrast, duplicate IDs or heading order. Use it after implementing and before delivering.

sources: W3C WAI-ARIA 1.2 and the Authoring Practices Guide

beforeAfter.prompt: Build me a confirmation modal in React for deleting an item.
beforeAfter.withoutSolver: A component with <div className="overlay"> and <div className="modal">, closed by an isOpen state, with "Cancel" and "Delete" buttons. No role or aria-modal, focus stays on the button that opened the modal, Tab moves through the page behind it, Esc does not close it and no tests are delivered. It ends with the generic suggestion: "add styles as needed".
beforeAfter.withSolver: Before coding: "Does the project already use a primitives library (Radix, React Aria)? Is the deletion asynchronous?". It delivers the native <dialog> with showModal() (focus trap and Esc for free), aria-labelledby pointing at the title, initial focus on "Cancel" (a destructive action does not get default focus), focus returning to the trigger on close, a "Delete" button with aria-disabled and the text "Deleting…" during the request, and the error in role="alert". Eight user-event tests (Esc closes, focus returns, a double click does not delete twice), all passing in run_tests.

beforeAfter.prompt: My sign-up form shows the errors in red but screen reader users are complaining. Can you fix it?
beforeAfter.withoutSolver: Suggests adding aria-label to the inputs and changing the error color to a darker red. Rewrites the form keeping the placeholders as labels and puts role="alert" on every error message, which makes the screen reader fire several announcements at once when the user submits an empty form.
beforeAfter.withSolver: Diagnosis as a list: a placeholder is not a label (replace it with <label htmlFor>), the error must be tied to the field with aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and role="alert" on each field produces stacked announcements. Fix: validation on submit, focus on the first invalid field (which already announces the label and the error), live revalidation only on fields that already show an error, and an optional error summary for long forms. It delivers the tests: toHaveAccessibleDescription on each error and toHaveFocus on the first invalid field.

beforeAfter.prompt: I need a login form in React. Should I block pasting in the password field to make it more secure?
beforeAfter.withoutSolver: Yes, blocking paste prevents passwords pasted from text files. Add onPaste with preventDefault on the password field.
beforeAfter.withSolver: Explains that blocking paste hurts password managers and goes against WCAG 2.2 success criterion 3.3.8, then delivers the login with the right autoComplete (username, current-password), a show-password button with aria-pressed, errors tied by aria-describedby, a generic message for invalid credentials and tests that prove all of it.

beforeAfter.prompt: Make my React landing page look polished, with gradients and an accent color the user can switch. Is it accessible?
beforeAfter.withoutSolver: Builds the page with white text on the accent gradient, reuses the accent color for the focus ring and the form borders, loops a background animation forever and answers "yes, it is accessible, it has alt text and labels" after a quick scan of the markup.
beforeAfter.withSolver: Plans separate tokens for text, focus ring and field border per theme and palette, darkens the gradient behind white text, and delivers a test that asserts the contrast of every token pair. Adds a visible Pause animations button (aria-pressed) besides prefers-reduced-motion and a live region for the Copied message. The summary says what was checked (tests, static check, computed contrast) and what was not (contrast over gradients, focus ring and layout need axe-core and a keyboard pass in a browser), instead of declaring the page accessible.

versions.notes: Visual accessibility and polish, learned from a real project where the static check passed and 11 contrast, focus, motion and status failures were still found by measuring. New knowledge: accessible design tokens (the brand color is not a text, focus or border color), contrast over gradients, focus ring, a pause control for animation (WCAG 2.2.2), live-region status messages, visual polish (scales, states, motion) and measured verification (axe-core per state, pixel contrast, keyboard pass). New styles template with a contrastRatio helper and tests. The method now plans the tokens and the verification, sends the complete files to the static check and reports exactly what was and was not verified, never calling a component accessible from static checks alone. Tools, onboarding and step structure did not change. The rating was not measured again on this version.

English becomes the primary language: method, knowledge base, templates and test cases were translated, and the Portuguese storefront text moved to locales/pt.json. The AI still answers in the user's language. The rating was measured again on this version (answers generated in English by an AI agent without seeing the checks).

Free trial: knowledge excerpts unlocked in the demo. Knowledge search in the trial now returns excerpts from some of each specialist's files (before, it returned none). The full knowledge base stays license-only; the method, templates and answers did not change.

Project setup in the specialist's memory (React version, framework, styling and component library). Knowledge base updated with source and date: React 19.3, React Compiler 1.0, WCAG 2.2 (authentication, target size, focus) and Vitest and Testing Library versions; fixes (WebAIM figure, scroll-padding technique). Component and test templates delivered by the server. More evaluation cases; the previous scores were withdrawn because they belonged to a different version.
Free trial with clear limits: what it unlocks and what only the license gives. Pay-per-use is gone: the specialist is now a lifetime license only.
First public version: 4-step method, a knowledge base of WAI-ARIA patterns, React 19 and Testing Library, server-side tests (Vitest) and an accessibility check. Guarantee available.
